analysis.one_liner: Orders the FTC to study whether drug middlemen inflate prescription prices and recommend fixes.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2023 but never received a Senate vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Federal Trade Commission to investigate pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that decide which drugs insurers cover and what pharmacies get paid — for practices that may raise drug prices, such as charging insurers more than they pay pharmacies and steering patients to their own pharmacies. The FTC would report its findings to Congress within a year and recommend laws to make the drug supply chain more competitive and transparent. It also requires a report on enforcement barriers against makers of sole-source drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who fill prescriptions could eventually benefit if the FTC study leads to rules that curb middleman markups and restore competition among pharmacies. Independent and community pharmacies, which are squeezed by pharmacy benefit manager payment practices, would also gain from the scrutiny and possible reforms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug buyers and local pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FTC to examine specific pharmacy benefit manager practices: charging payers more than it reimburses pharmacies, steering patients to pharmacies the managers own, using rival pharmacies' proprietary data for competitive advantage, and designing formularies to favor higher-cost drugs.

Requires the FTC to report on trends in competition across the drug supply chain and recommend policies to improve transparency and competition, deter anticompetitive behavior, and ensure consumers benefit from mergers.
Requires an interim report within 180 days and a final report within a year, so Congress gets findings and legislative recommendations on a defined timeline.
Also requires a report on complaints and enforcement capability regarding makers of sole-source drugs, and on legal or regulatory obstacles that contribute to high drug prices.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug supply chain intermediaries, whose business practices would face a federal antitrust investigation and possible future regulation. Taxpayers would fund the FTC's study, a modest cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug middlemen

drawbacks.text: The bill only commissions a study; it does not itself lower any drug price or ban any practice, and its findings would depend on Congress or the FTC acting later on the recommendations.
The FTC already has authority to study markets and enforce antitrust law, so the bill mainly adds a reporting deadline and a congressional mandate rather than new enforcement power.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is small — one government study — and the potential upside is real: the FTC has since found that three pharmacy benefit managers control a large share of the market, so a mandated review could have pushed concrete legislative fixes for prescription prices. But the bill is a first step, not relief itself, and without a floor vote it produced nothing.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it unanimously and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor business in March 2023, but Senate leaders never brought it up for a vote and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The bill had 21 cosponsors split evenly across parties — 10 Democrats, 10 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

On February 9, 2023, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment, and on March 1, 2023, it was reported by Senator Durbin and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — the list of bills awaiting floor consideration.
The bill received no further action after being placed on the calendar; no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it expired at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug supply chain intermediaries benefited, since the antitrust scrutiny of their pricing practices was never mandated, and no rules or competition reforms followed.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan from the start — 10 Democratic, 10 Republican, and 1 Independent cosponsor — and the Democratic-chaired Judiciary Committee reported the Republican sponsor's bill favorably; the bill never got far enough for a partisan floor vote.

industries.note: The bill targets PBMs' core practices — spread pricing, patient steering to affiliated pharmacies, use of rival pharmacies' data, and formulary design that favors costlier drugs — for a federal antitrust review and possible regulation. A study would not have cost them money immediately, but it could have laid groundwork for rules that cut their revenue from charging insurers more than they pay pharmacies.

The bill's focus on whether PBMs underpay non-affiliated pharmacies and steer patients away from them could improve reimbursement fairness for local pharmacies. Neighborhood pharmacies lose business when PBMs favor their own mail-order and retail operations.

industries.industry: Drug supply chain intermediaries and pharmacy services administrative organizations
industries.note: The FTC would study how these intermediaries integrate with suppliers and payers and whether consumers benefit from consolidation, putting their contracting practices under congressional and regulatory scrutiny.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers of sole-source drugs
industries.note: The bill requires a report on anticompetitive conduct complaints against makers of sole-source drugs and on enforcement obstacles, spotlighting manufacturers with no competition for a given drug. It imposes no direct obligation, but creates a record that could support future enforcement.
